outages.place: Paraná, including the North, West, Northwest, and other regions
outages.cause: Storms and two F1 tornadoes that damaged the electrical system with strong wind gusts, lightning, and fallen trees, according to Copel, with Simepar confirming the tornadoes
outages.affected: Copel, in a bulletin issued at 7:00 p.m. Brasília time Sunday, Nov 22 (4:00 p.m. CT), as reported by Umuarama News on Sunday and by TNOnline in an article published at 7:26 p.m. Brasília time Sunday (4:26 p.m. CT), said that it had already restored electricity to 98 percent of the consumer units affected by Friday's storms, and that approximately 8,800 consumer units remained without power across Paraná as of 7:00 p.m. Brasília time Sunday. Those reports, citing Copel, said the remaining outages at that bulletin were concentrated in the West (2,700 units), the North (2,200), the Northwest, including Umuarama and neighboring municipalities (1,500), the Southwest (1,100), the East, covering Curitiba, the metropolitan region, and the coast (767), and Centro-Sul (401). Copel said restoration work would continue without interruption until service was fully restored for all remaining customers. No official firm restoration time for all remaining customers was given. Leste News, in an article published at 1:25 a.m. Nov 23, restated that same Sunday 7:00 p.m. Copel bulletin of approximately 8,800 consumer units still without power and 98 percent already restored. An earlier Copel bulletin issued at 12:30 p.m. Brasília time Sunday, Nov 22 (9:30 a.m. CT), as reported by Umuarama News on Sunday, by OBemdito in an article published at 1:06 p.m. Brasília time Sunday (10:06 a.m. CT) and updated at 1:09 p.m. Brasília time Sunday (10:09 a.m. CT), by CBN Curitiba in an article updated at 2:24 p.m. Brasília time Sunday (11:24 a.m. CT), by Tribuna do Interior in an article published at 3:44 p.m. Brasília time Sunday (12:44 p.m. CT), and by Maringá Atual, had said that more than 96.5 percent of the affected consumer units had already been reconnected and that approximately 16,700 consumer units remained without power at that earlier hour, concentrated in the North (about 4,600 units), the West (4,100), the Northwest (about 3,500), the Southwest (about 2,300), the East (about 1,500), and Centro-Sul (568). An earlier Copel bulletin as of 6:30 p.m. Brasília time Saturday, Nov 21 (3:30 p.m. CT), as reported by CGN at 6:47 p.m. Brasília time Saturday (3:47 p.m. CT) and by Folha de Curitiba at 12:05 a.m. Brasília time Sunday, Nov 22 (9:05 p.m. CT Saturday), had said 54,246 consumer units remained without power and that 299,603 units, or 85 percent, had already been reconnected. An earlier noon Saturday Copel bulletin, as reported by Tribuna do Interior at 2:40 p.m. Brasília time Saturday (11:40 a.m. CT), said 80,588 units remained without power at that earlier hour, 273,261 had been restored (77.2 percent), and the peak had been 353,849 units at 8:02 p.m. Brasília time Friday, Nov 20 (5:02 p.m. CT Friday). Simepar confirmed two F1 tornadoes on Friday, Nov 20, one around 3:00 p.m. Brasília time (noon CT Friday) in the Vila Yolanda neighborhood of Foz do Iguaçu and another around 6:00 p.m. Brasília time (3:00 p.m. CT Friday) in Manoel Ribas, with estimated winds of 117 to 180 km/h. No later official Copel remaining-customer count after the 7:00 p.m. Brasília time Sunday bulletin was found as of 5:55 AM CT Monday, Nov 23 (8:55 a.m. Brasília time Monday, Nov 23).
outages.start: Afternoon and evening of Friday, Nov 20, 2026 (Brasília time), when storms and two F1 tornadoes hit Paraná; the peak of 353,849 consumer units was recorded at 8:02 p.m. Brasília time Friday (5:02 p.m. CT Friday), according to Copel's Saturday noon bulletin as reported by Tribuna do Interior

outages.cause: Rolling and emergency blackouts after Russian attacks on energy infrastructure, including a large-scale attack on Nov 20 and further strikes reported on Nov 21 and into Nov 22 and Nov 23. Ukrenergo said planned outage schedules would be in effect around the clock on Monday, Nov 23, in parts of the country because of those attacks
outages.affected: Ukrenergo, as reported by UNN at 10:11 a.m. Kyiv time Monday, Nov 23 (2:11 a.m. CT), and by Slovo i Dilo at 12:38 p.m. EET Monday (4:38 a.m. CT), said that restoration work continued throughout the night in Odesa and Dnipropetrovsk oblasts, where energy infrastructure was significantly damaged as a result of Russian attacks; that the situation in Odesa Oblast had been partially stabilized and electricity supply to critical infrastructure in Odesa had been restored; and that the situation in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast remained significantly more difficult, with hourly outage schedules in effect in the region. Those Monday reports, citing Ukrenergo, also said that on Monday, Nov 23, planned restrictions would be in effect around the clock in some regions of Ukraine: capacity-limitation schedules for industry, and hourly outage schedules of 1 to 4 queues for all categories of consumers. Vidomo, in an article dated 10:59 a.m. Monday, Nov 23 (2:59 a.m. CT if Kyiv time / EET), citing Ukraine's Energy Ministry and First Deputy Energy Minister Artem Nekrasov, said that as of the morning of Nov 23, some consumers remained without power in the Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Zhytomyr, Odesa, Poltava, Sumy, and Kharkiv regions because of shelling and combat; that in most regions hourly outage schedules and capacity restrictions for industry were in effect; and that in Kharkiv region emergency outages had been applied because of a voltage drop in the high-voltage network. The same report, citing the Energy Ministry, said Russian forces had carried out 100 targeted attacks on Ukraine's energy and oil-and-gas infrastructure in the past week, with 224 incidents of damage to facilities recorded in all, and that repeated shelling and frequent air-raid alerts were substantially slowing repair crews. An earlier Sunday night Ukrenergo statement, as reported by Censor.NET at 10:24 p.m. EET Sunday, Nov 22 (2:24 p.m. CT), by UNIAN at 11:13 p.m. EET Sunday (3:13 p.m. CT), by Focus at 11:00 p.m. EET Sunday (3:00 p.m. CT), and by 24tv, had said that on Monday, Nov 23, planned electricity outages would be in effect around the clock in parts of the country: hourly outage schedules of 1 to 3.5 groups, or queues, for all categories of consumers, and capacity-restriction schedules for industry. UNIAN, in that Sunday night report, said those 1 to 3.5 queues amounted to approximately 4 to 16 hours a day for household consumers. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, in his Sunday evening address as reported by Ukrinform at 9:09 p.m. EET Sunday, Nov 22 (1:09 p.m. CT) and by 24tv, said Russian forces were now using a tactic of destroying networks and transmission lines in an effort to cut Odesa, Odesa region, and Dnipropetrovsk region off from energy sources, that the situation there was very difficult and that there were significant outages, and that repair crews were also working in Dnipro, Kamianske, Kharkiv region, and Poltava region. No official nationwide customer count was found as of 5:55 AM CT Monday, Nov 23 (1:55 p.m. EET Monday).
outages.updated: Nov 23, 2026, Ukrenergo Monday morning update via UNN 10:11 a.m. Kyiv time Monday, Nov 23 (= 2:11 a.m. CT) and Slovo i Dilo 12:38 p.m. EET Monday (= 4:38 a.m. CT), on overnight restoration work in Odesa and Dnipropetrovsk oblasts, a partially stabilized situation and restored critical infrastructure in Odesa, a significantly more difficult situation with hourly schedules in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, and Monday all-day planned restrictions of 1 to 4 queues in some regions; Energy Ministry and First Deputy Energy Minister Artem Nekrasov via Vidomo 10:59 a.m. Monday (= 2:59 a.m. CT if Kyiv time / EET), on consumers still without power as of Monday morning in the Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Zhytomyr, Odesa, Poltava, Sumy, and Kharkiv regions, emergency outages in Kharkiv region because of a high-voltage voltage drop, and 100 attacks on energy and oil-and-gas infrastructure in the past week with 224 damage incidents; earlier Sunday night Ukrenergo schedules of 1 to 3.5 queues via Censor.NET 10:24 p.m. EET Sunday, Nov 22 (= 2:24 p.m. CT), UNIAN 11:13 p.m. EET Sunday (= 3:13 p.m. CT), Focus, and 24tv, with UNIAN saying those queues amounted to approximately 4 to 16 hours a day; President Volodymyr Zelenskyy Sunday evening address via Ukrinform 9:09 p.m. EET Sunday (= 1:09 p.m. CT) and 24tv; rechecked 5:55 AM CT Monday, Nov 23 (1:55 p.m. EET Monday), no official nationwide customer count found

outages.place: Odesa and parts of Odesa district
outages.cause: Repeated Russian attacks on high-voltage transmission networks and other energy facilities critical to the region, including a strike on a DTEK Odeski Elektromerezhi energy facility on the morning of Nov 20. Ukrenergo said on Monday, Nov 23, that the situation in Odesa Oblast had been partially stabilized and that electricity supply to critical infrastructure in Odesa had been restored, after main power grids suffered serious damage; Odesa regional governor Oleh Kiper said emergency outages without schedules were still being applied because the damaged equipment could not yet supply all consumers at once
outages.affected: Odesa regional governor Oleh Kiper, as reported by Censor.NET at 12:35 p.m. EET Monday, Nov 23 (4:35 a.m. CT), by UNN at 10:11 a.m. Kyiv time Monday (2:11 a.m. CT), and by Slovo i Dilo at 12:38 p.m. EET Monday (4:38 a.m. CT), said the electricity-supply situation in Odesa region remained difficult but that measures were being taken to stabilize it; that as a result of Russian attacks, Ukrenergo's main transmission network supplying Odesa and surrounding communities had sustained significant damage, and that given the scale of the destruction, restoration would take time; that all critical-infrastructure facilities and some consumers had already been energized; and that emergency outages without schedules were still being applied in Odesa District, including Odesa, because the damaged equipment did not yet allow electricity to be supplied to all consumers at the same time. Kiper, in those reports, said there was water in all districts of the city, though some apartment buildings might experience interruptions in water pumping; that of 11 large boiler houses, 9 were already operating, while 2 boiler houses and the combined heat and power plant were being brought online; that 130 small boiler houses were operating and 18 more would be launched shortly; and that heat had already been supplied to 186,000 subscribers, while about 79,000 consumers were temporarily without heating. Ukrenergo, as reported by UNN and Slovo i Dilo on Monday, said the situation in Odesa Oblast had been partially stabilized and that electricity supply to critical infrastructure in Odesa had been restored, after restoration work continued throughout the night. UNN also reported that Odesa City Military Administration head Serhii Lysak said in the morning that the past two days had been a test for Odesa and that, because of the enemy strike on the region's energy infrastructure, the city had been left without electricity, heating, or water; that deputy head Serhii Krasilenko said water supply had already been restored in all districts of Odesa thanks to backup power; and that, according to the Odesa City Council, as of the morning of Nov 23 the city's electric transport had been temporarily suspended, while schools and kindergartens where heating was restored would operate as usual on Tuesday, Nov 24. No official remaining-electricity-customer count was given in those Monday reports. Earlier Friday DTEK figures, cited in prior official and local reporting, had put remaining households at 8,000 families after the morning attack, after an earlier Friday morning figure of 41,000 households. No official remaining-electricity-customer count after those earlier Friday DTEK figures was found as of 5:55 AM CT Monday, Nov 23 (1:55 p.m. EET Monday).
outages.updated: Nov 23, 2026, Odesa regional governor Oleh Kiper via Censor.NET 12:35 p.m. EET Monday, Nov 23 (= 4:35 a.m. CT), UNN 10:11 a.m. Kyiv time Monday (= 2:11 a.m. CT), and Slovo i Dilo 12:38 p.m. EET Monday (= 4:38 a.m. CT), on a still-difficult supply situation, emergency outages without schedules still being applied in Odesa District including Odesa, all critical infrastructure and some consumers already energized, water in all districts with possible pumping interruptions in some apartment buildings, 9 of 11 large boiler houses operating and 2 plus the CHP being brought online, heat already supplied to 186,000 subscribers, and about 79,000 consumers temporarily without heating; Ukrenergo Monday statement via UNN and Slovo i Dilo that the Odesa Oblast situation had been partially stabilized and that critical infrastructure in Odesa had been restored after overnight repair work; Odesa City Military Administration head Serhii Lysak and deputy head Serhii Krasilenko, and the Odesa City Council, via UNN, on the city having been left without electricity, heating, or water, on water supply restored in all districts with backup power, on electric transport temporarily suspended as of Monday morning, and on schools and kindergartens with restored heating to operate as usual on Tuesday, Nov 24; earlier Friday DTEK remaining 8,000 families after the morning attack and earlier Friday morning 41,000-household figure; rechecked 5:55 AM CT Monday, Nov 23 (1:55 p.m. EET Monday), no official remaining-electricity-customer count after the earlier Friday DTEK figures found

outages.place: Dnipro and parts of Dnipropetrovsk region, including Dniprovskyi, Samarivskyi, Kamianske, and Pavlohrad districts
outages.cause: Russian attacks that significantly damaged energy infrastructure in the region, according to Ukrenergo and Ukraine's Energy Ministry. First Deputy Energy Minister Artem Nekrasov said network restrictions were introduced to avoid accidents from overloaded equipment, and regional officials said emergency outages were in effect in Dnipro and several districts
outages.affected: Ukrenergo, as reported by UNN at 10:11 a.m. Kyiv time Monday, Nov 23 (2:11 a.m. CT) and by Slovo i Dilo at 12:38 p.m. EET Monday (4:38 a.m. CT), said the situation in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast remained significantly more difficult, that hourly outage schedules were in effect in the region, and that power engineers were continuing work to reduce the scope of the restrictions as quickly as possible, after restoration work continued throughout the night where energy infrastructure was significantly damaged as a result of Russian attacks. Vidomo, in an article dated 10:59 a.m. Monday, Nov 23 (2:59 a.m. CT if Kyiv time / EET), citing Dnipropetrovsk regional council head Mykola Lukashuk, said that as of Nov 23 emergency outages remained in effect in Dnipro and in the Dniprovskyi, Samarivskyi, Kamianske, and Pavlohrad districts, and that DTEK hourly outage schedules were not being applied in those communities. The same report said that for customers of the Central Energy Company (CEK), the region's other distribution-system operator, an hourly outage schedule was in effect on Nov 23, and that a separate schedule had been formed for part of the city of Pavlohrad. Vidomo, citing First Deputy Energy Minister Artem Nekrasov, said the situation in the energy system of Dnipropetrovsk and Odesa regions remained difficult because of large-scale destruction of energy facilities that supply those regions; that critical infrastructure had been energized; that network restrictions had been introduced in Dnipropetrovsk region to avoid accidents from overloaded equipment; and that electricity was being returned to consumers in stages. The Energy Ministry, as reported by Vidomo, also said that as of the morning of Nov 23 some consumers in Dnipropetrovsk region remained without power because of shelling and combat, and that a gas-infrastructure facility in the region had been attacked the previous day, injuring three workers. No official customer count was given in those reports as of 5:55 AM CT Monday, Nov 23 (1:55 p.m. EET Monday).
outages.updated: Nov 23, 2026, Ukrenergo via UNN 10:11 a.m. Kyiv time Monday, Nov 23 (= 2:11 a.m. CT) and Slovo i Dilo 12:38 p.m. EET Monday (= 4:38 a.m. CT), saying the Dnipropetrovsk Oblast situation remained significantly more difficult, with hourly outage schedules in effect and overnight restoration work after significant damage from Russian attacks; Dnipropetrovsk regional council head Mykola Lukashuk via Vidomo 10:59 a.m. Monday (= 2:59 a.m. CT if Kyiv time / EET), on emergency outages remaining in effect in Dnipro and in the Dniprovskyi, Samarivskyi, Kamianske, and Pavlohrad districts where DTEK hourly schedules were not being applied, with an hourly schedule in effect for Central Energy Company (CEK) customers and a separate schedule for part of Pavlohrad; First Deputy Energy Minister Artem Nekrasov and the Energy Ministry via Vidomo, on network restrictions to avoid accidents from overloaded equipment, critical infrastructure energized, power being returned in stages, some consumers still without power as of Monday morning because of shelling and combat, and a previous-day attack on a gas-infrastructure facility that injured three workers; rechecked 5:55 AM CT Monday, Nov 23 (1:55 p.m. EET Monday), no official customer count found

outages.place: Kurdistan Region, including Erbil, Sulaymaniyah, Duhok, Bazian, and Chamchamal
outages.cause: Suspected drone attack on the Khor Mor gas field on the night of Nov 8, 2026, which halted gas production that supplies much of the region's electricity generation. Dana Gas, the field's operator, later said the facility had sustained significant damage and could produce no gas
outages.affected: Kurdistan24, in a Nov 22, 2026 report, said a trilateral meeting of the Kurdistan Regional Government, Iraq's Oil Ministry, and Dana Gas was expected within the next two days to discuss procedures for restarting natural gas production and delivery from the Khor Mor field. A KRG source told Kurdistan24 that a restart depends on Dana Gas obtaining security approval so it can resume operations, and that official results of investigations into the Nov 8 attack had not yet been made public. The same report said the Nov 8 drone attack in Sulaimani province caused a large fire and stopped gas production entirely, with no casualties, and that the stoppage cut 2,500 to 2,800 megawatts of electricity in the Kurdistan Region and reduced power-supply hours by five to six hours a day. That account is consistent with earlier official figures: Al Jazeera, on Nov 9, citing Iraqi and Kurdish officials and the official Iraqi News Agency, said the attack left more than 70 percent of the Kurdish region without power and, citing Omed Ahmed, spokesperson for the KRG Ministry of Electricity, that it suspended gas supply to power plants in Erbil, Sulaymaniyah, Bazian, Chamchamal, and Duhok and knocked between 2,500 and 2,800 megawatts off the grid. Rudaw later quoted Ahmed as saying authorities had increased generation from approximately 1,000 megawatts immediately after the attack to 1,550 megawatts, of which 50 megawatts were reserved for essential facilities and factories, leaving 1,500 megawatts for residents and raising daily public electricity supply to six to eight hours; Ahmed said the electricity then available covered only 40 percent of demand, leaving a 60 percent shortfall, and that no date had been established for production to resume. Rudaw's article image assets for that report are dated Nov 13, 2026. 964media, in a Nov 15 report, quoted Ahmed as saying that no timeframe had been set for supplies to return to normal and that within 48 hours of the attack generation had been increased from 1,000 megawatts to nearly 1,650 megawatts. Dana Gas, in a Nov 14 clarification later restated in coverage including a Kurdistan24 report, said the facility had sustained significant damage and that no gas could currently be produced. The Insight International, in a Nov 21 report citing private-generator officials who spoke to Rudaw on Saturday, Nov 21, said the public grid remained weak because of the gas shortfall and that neighborhood generators were still running for most of the day in Erbil, Sulaimani, and Duhok. The New Region, in a Nov 22, 2026 report, said delegations from the Kurdistan Regional Government's natural resources ministry and from Iraq's oil ministry were set to meet Dana Gas on Monday, Nov 23, to discuss resuming gas production and supplies to power plants; that Dana Gas was expected to insist on security guarantees against further attacks; and that if an agreement were reached on Monday, a specialized Turkish company would begin repairs estimated to take six days. No official customer count was given. No later official ministry generation figure, and no official confirmation that Khor Mor production had resumed or that a Monday agreement on repairs had been reached, was found as of 5:55 AM CT Monday, Nov 23 (2:55 p.m. Iraq time Monday).
outages.etr: No official firm restoration time was given. The New Region, in a Nov 22, 2026 report, said delegations from Erbil and Baghdad were set to meet Dana Gas on Monday, Nov 23, to discuss resuming production, that Dana Gas was expected to insist on security guarantees against further attacks, and that if an agreement were reached on Monday, a specialized Turkish company would begin repairs estimated to take six days. A KRG source told Kurdistan24 on Nov 22 that a restart depends on Dana Gas obtaining security approval. As of the latest official statements found, Khor Mor production had not been confirmed as having resumed, and no firm date had been established for production to resume.
outages.updated: Nov 22–23, 2026, The New Region dated Nov 22, 2026, on a planned Monday, Nov 23, meeting of Erbil and Baghdad delegations with Dana Gas on restarting Khor Mor production, with Dana Gas expected to seek security guarantees and, if an agreement were reached Monday, a specialized Turkish company to begin repairs estimated at six days; earlier Kurdistan24 on a planned trilateral meeting within two days on restarting Khor Mor production, with a KRG source saying a restart depends on Dana Gas obtaining security approval, and on the field remaining shut after the Nov 8 attack that cut 2,500 to 2,800 megawatts and reduced supply hours by five to six hours a day; earlier Al Jazeera Nov 9 citing Iraqi and Kurdish officials and INA; KRG electricity ministry figures via Rudaw (article image assets dated Nov 13) and 964media Nov 15; Dana Gas still-shut statement of Nov 14; The Insight International Nov 21, citing private-generator officials who spoke to Rudaw on Saturday, Nov 21, on the public-grid shortfall continuing; rechecked 5:55 AM CT Monday, Nov 23 (2:55 p.m. Iraq time Monday), no later official generation figure or confirmation that Khor Mor production had resumed or that a Monday repair agreement had been reached found

outages.place: Donetsk, Makiivka, Yenakiieve, Khartsyzk, Zuhres, Torez, Snizhne, and nearby districts
outages.cause: Attacks on energy infrastructure, including a massive attack on the night of Nov 22, 2026, according to occupation officials, who said attacks on energy facilities were repeated the following night and that new outages were added to the effects of earlier damage; occupation officials also described a power deficit and forced temporary outages to prevent accidents
outages.affected: The occupation Ministry of Coal and Energy, as reported by RIA Novosti at 12:50 p.m. Monday, Nov 23 (3:50 a.m. CT if Moscow time), and by DNR News at 9:48 a.m. Monday (12:48 a.m. CT if Moscow time), said that as of the morning slightly more than 207,000 subscribers remained without electricity after attacks on the energy system, and that restoration work was continuing despite the threat of further strikes. RIA Novosti, citing the ministry, said attacks on energy facilities had been repeated the previous night, that no specialists had been injured, and that partial outages had been recorded in Donetsk, Makiivka, the Amvrosiivka, Volnovakha, Telmanove, Shakhtarsk, and Yasynuvata municipal districts, and in Khartsyzk, Zuhres, Torez, Snizhne, and Yenakiieve. The ministry, as reported by RIA Novosti, also said that after each new attack energy workers had to reconnect customers who had only recently had electricity restored, and that damage to energy facilities was also causing a shortage of available capacity, leading to forced temporary outages to prevent accidents. Vedomosti, in a Nov 23, 2026 report, citing Donetsk occupation mayor Alexei Kulemzin and data from the Donetskenergo branch of the South-West Electric Grid Company, said 114,648 subscribers remained without electricity in Donetsk city, that partial outages had affected all districts of the city, and that 551 transformer substations were de-energized; Kulemzin did not give a time for full restoration. An earlier Sunday statement by occupation government head Andrei Chertkov, as reported by DNR News on Nov 22, had said more than 279,000 subscribers were without power after attacks, including partial outages in Donetsk, Makiivka, Mariupol, Yenakiieve, Debaltseve, Torez, and Snizhne and in settlements of several municipal districts. Chertkov, as reported by DNR News at 11:41 a.m. Monday, Nov 23 (2:41 a.m. CT if Moscow time), said rolling outages in the territory were mainly linked to damage to energy hubs and could not always be forecast in advance. No official firm restoration time for all remaining subscribers was given in the Monday reports as of 5:55 AM CT Monday, Nov 23 (2:55 p.m. Moscow time Monday).
outages.start: Night of Sunday, Nov 22, 2026, local time, for the attack described by occupation officials; occupation officials said attacks on energy facilities were repeated the following night; other partial outages in the region were already being reported
outages.etr: Occupation government head Andrei Chertkov, as reported by DNR News at 5:45 p.m. Sunday, Nov 22 (8:45 a.m. CT if Moscow time), said restoration of the damaged energy center would take roughly two to three weeks. Donetsk occupation mayor Alexei Kulemzin, as reported by Vedomosti on Nov 23, did not give a time for full restoration of electricity in the city. No official firm restoration time was given for all remaining subscribers.
outages.updated: Nov 23, 2026, occupation Ministry of Coal and Energy via RIA Novosti 12:50 p.m. Monday, Nov 23 (= 3:50 a.m. CT if Moscow time) and DNR News 9:48 a.m. Monday (= 12:48 a.m. CT if Moscow time), saying slightly more than 207,000 subscribers remained without electricity as of Monday morning, that attacks on energy facilities had been repeated the previous night, and listing partial outages in Donetsk, Makiivka, the Amvrosiivka, Volnovakha, Telmanove, Shakhtarsk, and Yasynuvata municipal districts, and in Khartsyzk, Zuhres, Torez, Snizhne, and Yenakiieve, with forced temporary outages also attributed to a shortage of available capacity; Vedomosti Nov 23 report citing Donetsk occupation mayor Alexei Kulemzin and Donetskenergo on 114,648 subscribers without electricity in Donetsk city, partial outages in all districts of the city, and 551 de-energized transformer substations, with no full-restoration time given; occupation government head Andrei Chertkov via DNR News 11:41 a.m. Monday (= 2:41 a.m. CT if Moscow time) on rolling outages linked to damaged energy hubs that could not always be forecast in advance; earlier Sunday Chertkov figure of more than 279,000 subscribers via DNR News Nov 22, and his Sunday estimate of roughly two to three weeks to restore the damaged energy center; rechecked 5:55 AM CT Monday, Nov 23 (2:55 p.m. Moscow time Monday)

outages.place: Crimea and Sevastopol, including Yevpatoria, Dzhankoy, Bilohirsk, Feodosia, Alushta, and other districts
outages.cause: A power-capacity shortage after strikes on transmission networks outside the peninsula, according to occupation sources. Krymenergo said a consumption-restriction regime was introduced on Monday morning, Nov 23, by command of the federal system operator, and later Monday notices described further rolling outages of about three hours in multiple districts
outages.affected: Krymenergo, as reported by RIA Novosti Crimea at 10:24 a.m. Monday, Nov 23 (1:24 a.m. CT if Moscow time), said electricity supply had been temporarily restricted in several cities and districts because of the introduced consumption limits, and that the approximate duration of the outages was three hours. That report, citing Krymenergo, listed outages or scheduled cuts in the Pervomaiske, Saky, Bilohirsk, Bakhchisaray, Dzhankoy city and district, Sovetskyi, Lenine, and Kirovske districts, partial outages in Chornomorske district, partial outages in the center of Feodosia and in the area of Poleva and Volodarskoho streets, and additional streets in Yevpatoria. Alushta administration head Galina Ogneva, as quoted in the same report, said a rolling-outage schedule was in effect throughout the municipality because of insufficient available capacity. Rossiyskaya Gazeta, in an article dated 10:03 a.m. Monday, Nov 23 (1:03 a.m. CT if Moscow time), also said eight rural districts were partially without power — Saky, Bilohirsk, Bakhchisaray, and Dzhankoy, and later Chornomorske, Lenine, Kirovske, and Sovetskyi — with an approximate restoration time of three hours, and that a limited-consumption regime continued in Crimea and Sevastopol; the same report said Sevastopol was operating on a two-through-six schedule, with two hours of electricity alternating with six hours without power. A later Krymenergo notice, as posted by Crimea-News at 2:21 p.m. Monday, Nov 23 (5:21 a.m. CT if Moscow time), said that from approximately 2:30 p.m. local time Monday (5:30 a.m. CT) electricity would be cut in Lenine district in Oktyabrske, Baherove, Ivanivka, Novoselivka, and Gornostaevka, and partially in Fontan and Pryozerne, for an approximate duration of three hours. An earlier Krymenergo update, as reported by RIA Novosti Crimea at 8:18 a.m. Monday, updated at 8:37 a.m. Monday (11:18 p.m. and 11:37 p.m. CT Sunday, Nov 22, if Moscow time), had said a consumption-restriction regime was introduced Monday morning by command of the federal system operator, with outages expected to last about three to six hours, and had listed Monday morning outages in more than 20 localities in Dzhankoy district and in streets and garden associations in Yevpatoria. Occupation sources have said peninsula-wide interruptions began Oct 24, 2026, after strikes on transmission networks outside the peninsula. No official customer count was given in those Monday reports as of 5:55 AM CT Monday, Nov 23 (2:55 p.m. Moscow time Monday).

outages.cause: Generation-capacity deficit in the national electric system. UNE's Sunday bulletin said units 1 and 2 of CTE Santa Cruz and unit 2 of CTE Felton were in breakdown, and that unit 3 of CTE Santa Cruz, unit 5 of CTE Nuevitas, unit 5 of CTE Renté, and unit 1 of CTE Felton were in maintenance, with thermal-generation limitations of 423 MW
outages.affected: UNE's Sunday bulletin, published by Granma at 10:11 a.m. Cuba time Sunday, Nov 22 (9:11 a.m. CT) and also reported by Directorio Cubano at 8:32 a.m. Sunday, said service had been affected by a generation-capacity deficit throughout all 24 hours on Saturday, Nov 21, and that the affectation continued through the early morning, with a maximum affectation of 1,778 MW recorded at 6:50 p.m. Cuba time Saturday (5:50 p.m. CT Saturday). It said solar-photovoltaic parks produced 3,474 MWh on Saturday, with a maximum of 540 MW delivered in the midday period. At 6:00 a.m. Cuba time Sunday (5:00 a.m. CT), the bulletin said SEN availability was 1,037 MW against demand of 2,255 MW, with 1,220 MW affected. For the midday period it estimated an affectation of 1,200 MW. UNE estimated that unit 2 of CTE Santa Cruz would enter for the evening peak with 80 MW, and it forecast availability of 1,117 MW against a maximum demand of 2,800 MW, a deficit of 1,683 MW, and, if those conditions held, an affectation of 1,713 MW at the peak. The bulletin said units 1 and 2 of CTE Santa Cruz and unit 2 of CTE Felton were in breakdown, and that unit 3 of CTE Santa Cruz, unit 5 of CTE Nuevitas, unit 5 of CTE Renté, and unit 1 of CTE Felton were in maintenance, with thermal-generation limitations of 423 MW. CiberCuba, in a page updated at 12:12 p.m. Cuba time Sunday (11:12 a.m. CT), presented the same official UNE Sunday figures, said there was no total collapse of the national grid recorded, and continued to show local Havana circuit reports during the late morning. Official UNE sources did not report a total collapse of the national grid. CiberCuba, in a page updated at 6:14 p.m. Cuba time Sunday (5:14 p.m. CT), still presented the same official UNE Sunday morning forecast of a 1,713 MW evening-peak affectation and said there was no total collapse of the national grid recorded. That page also listed Empresa Eléctrica de La Habana local circuit outage reports around 5:56 p.m. Cuba time Sunday (4:56 p.m. CT), attributed to a generation-capacity deficit. CiberCuba, in its Nov 23 daily summary, citing Empresa Eléctrica de La Habana, said that at 3:01 a.m. Cuba time Monday, Nov 23 (2:01 a.m. CT), 128 MW were affected across 53 circuits in Havana, and that at 6:00 a.m. Cuba time Monday (5:00 a.m. CT), 60 distribution circuits remained affected and the deficit affectation was 126 MW, attributed to a generation-capacity deficit. No official Sunday evening-peak actual from UNE, and no official Monday national UNE bulletin, was found as of 5:55 AM CT Monday, Nov 23 (6:55 a.m. Cuba time Monday).

outages.cause: Planned electricity restrictions that Tavanir said began Sunday, Nov 22, 2026, because fuel shortages were disrupting power generation
outages.affected: The National, in an article dated November 23, 2026, and marked updated at 5:00 AM, said Iran had begun imposing scheduled power cuts on consumers because of difficulties supplying fuel to power plants, according to state electricity company Tavanir. The article quoted Tavanir chief executive Mohammad Allahdad telling state television on Sunday that the restrictions were initially expected to last up to two hours every other day, rising to two hours daily if temperatures dropped further, and that, given the country's fuel-supply conditions, the electricity sector would be forced to impose distribution restrictions from Sunday. The National also quoted Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, as reported by the Isna news agency, saying the attack on the country's gas infrastructure had aggravated the situation and that difficulties should therefore be expected this winter. Iran International, in a report dated 1:17 p.m. GMT Sunday, Nov 22 (7:17 a.m. CT), said scheduled power cuts had resumed across Iran, disrupting homes, businesses, and schools. It said people in Tehran, Isfahan, Shiraz, Mashhad, Yazd, Kermanshah, and Ardabil had reported hours-long outages, often without notice, in messages sent to Iran International on Sunday, and that the disruptions had also affected water supplies and internet access. The report said Mohammad Allahdad, chief executive of state electricity company Tavanir, announced Saturday that residential and commercial power restrictions would begin November 22 because of fuel shortages at power plants, and that outages could last two hours every other day, increasing to two hours daily if temperatures fall further. RFE/RL, in a report dated midnight CET Sunday, Nov 22 (5:00 p.m. CT Saturday), said the cuts started Nov 22 and quoted Allahdad telling state television that the outages are expected to last up to two hours a day depending on location. Nour News, in a report dated 8:09 a.m. Iran time Sunday, Nov 22, or 1 Azar 1405 (10:39 p.m. CT Saturday), and Eghtesad Online, in a report dated 8:29 a.m. Iran time Sunday (10:59 p.m. CT Saturday) that cited Nour News, said planned electricity restrictions began today and, citing the Tavanir chief executive, that the new restrictions may take the form of a two-hour outage over two days, or a maximum of two hours each day, that the timing is not fixed and may change with network conditions, and that customers would be informed through the Bargh-e Man system and app, the Bale messenger app, and text messages. Tavanir had announced on Saturday, Nov 21, that planned electricity restrictions on households and businesses would begin on Sunday, Nov 22, because fuel shortages were disrupting power generation, according to Iran International in a report dated 5:11 p.m. GMT Saturday, Nov 21 (11:11 a.m. CT), and to RFE/RL. Anar News, in a report updated at 12:05 a.m. UTC Sunday, Nov 22 (6:05 p.m. CT Saturday), citing BBC Persian, also said planned power outages began in Iran on Sunday, Nov 22, because of fuel shortages at power plants. No official customer count was given in those reports. No official nationwide remaining-customer count was found as of 5:55 AM CT Monday, Nov 23 (3:25 p.m. Iran time Monday).

outages.cause: Drone attacks on power stations and other electricity infrastructure during the war between the Rapid Support Forces and the Sudanese Armed Forces
outages.affected: No official customer count. Drop Site News, in a Nov 20, 2026 report from Khartoum, said a particularly intense wave of drone strikes at the end of October and into November targeting power stations, fuel supplies, and electricity infrastructure had brought the country's power grid to the brink of collapse, and that two weeks after the wave of attacks, major substations remained out of service. Shaker Ismail, an engineer with the Sudanese Electricity Company, told Drop Site that repairing some of the country's most important power facilities could take months or longer, that high-capacity transformers and digital control systems had been damaged, and that replacement transformers must be manufactured to order abroad. Ismail said the Um Dabakir thermal power plant in White Nile State was badly damaged in an Oct 29 strike and forced to shut down, and that the Al-Markhiyat substation west of Omdurman was put out of service after an Oct 27 strike; he said affected areas continued to experience prolonged outages and scheduled power cuts as of this week. The report said the Sudan Electricity Holding Company and Ministry of Energy had yet to publicly announce the restoration of the major facilities damaged in the attacks. A United Nations report published Nov 17, issued in Geneva and posted on the UN in Sudan website, said that in just over two weeks between Oct 20 and Nov 4, 29 drone strikes, attributed to the Rapid Support Forces, hit electricity facilities and fuel stations across 11 states, triggering widespread power blackouts and further fuel shortages affecting millions far from the conflict frontlines. An earlier Al Jazeera Nov 15 feature said there is no clear schedule for the resulting power cuts, which can last anywhere between six hours and a day, and, citing The Associated Press, said repeated drone attacks on power stations have seen electricity generation fall from about 4,400 megawatts before the war to about 1,100 MW. Residents and a small-business owner in Port Sudan described prolonged, unreliable cuts, including outages lasting more than 24 hours. Al-Ghad Al-Sudani, in a report last updated Nov 22, 2026, said explosions and drone flights returned to Khartoum on Sunday morning, Nov 22, amid reports of attacks on military sites in various parts of the capital, and that the attacks coincided with power outages in large parts of the city; the report did not give a customer count or independently establish the cause of that outage. No later official national customer count or restoration timetable was found as of 5:55 AM CT Monday, Nov 23.
